lesson.title: The Power That Actually Does Work: Real Power in AC Circuits
lesson.summary: Real power P, measured in watts, is the portion of an AC circuit's power that is actually converted into heat, light, or mechanical work, distinct from the larger apparent power the source must supply.
lesson.body:
Instantaneous power in any circuit is simply p(t) = v(t)i(t), and in an AC circuit that product oscillates constantly, sometimes even swinging negative when energy is momentarily flowing back into the source rather than out of it. What a light bulb, a motor, or a heater actually cares about is not this instant-by-instant wiggle but its average over a complete cycle, and that average is exactly what we call real power, P, also called average power or active power, measured in watts. In a purely resistive circuit, voltage and current stay perfectly in phase, p(t) never goes negative, and the average works out to simply P = Vrms times Irms.

Once reactance enters the picture and current shifts out of phase with voltage by an angle theta, part of that instantaneous power spends part of every cycle flowing backward, energy sloshing into an inductor's magnetic field or a capacitor's electric field and then returning, doing no net work. Averaging over a full cycle, only a fraction of the raw Vrms times Irms product survives as real power: P = Vrms Irms cos(theta). That factor, cos(theta), is precisely the power factor, the ratio of real power actually delivered to the apparent power the source appears to be supplying. A power factor of 1 means every bit of apparent power becomes real power; a power factor below 1 means some of it is just sloshing back and forth uselessly.

Suppose a 120 V RMS supply feeds a motor drawing 10 A RMS, with current lagging voltage by theta = 30 degrees, typical of an inductive load. The apparent power is S = Vrms Irms = 120 times 10 = 1200 VA. The power factor is cos(30 degrees), about 0.8660, so the real power is P = 1200 times 0.8660, about 1039.2 W. Even though the source is supplying 1200 volt-amps worth of voltage and current, only about 1039 watts of that actually turns the motor's shaft or produces heat; the rest is reactive power shuttling in and out of the motor's windings every cycle without being consumed.

The averaging step can be seen directly from the trigonometry. Writing v(t) = Vm cos(wt) and i(t) = Im cos(wt - theta), their product expands, using a standard product-to-sum identity, into a constant term plus a term oscillating at twice the original frequency: p(t) = (VmIm/2)[cos(theta) + cos(2wt - theta)]. The oscillating term averages to exactly zero over any whole number of cycles, leaving only (VmIm/2)cos(theta), which equals Vrms Irms cos(theta) once you substitute Vrms = Vm/sqrt(2) and Irms = Im/sqrt(2). That surviving constant term is real power, and it is exactly what a utility's kilowatt-hour meter is built to track, integrated over time rather than the raw, oscillating apparent power that the voltage and current amplitudes alone would suggest.

Real power is also the quantity that never lies about energy consumption, which is why every appliance rating you actually pay for, watts on a light bulb, kilowatts on a stove, is a real power figure rather than an apparent power one, and why the gap between the two, governed entirely by the power factor, is worth tracking closely in any circuit with significant reactance.
